blocks.prompt: 7 A triangle has vertices at \(A(4, 1)\), \(B(-2, 5)\) and \(C(0, -3)\). Find the vertices of the reflected triangle over the \(y\)-axis using a transformation matrix.
blocks.explanation:
A reflection question: use the transformation (reflection) matrix of the \(y\)-axis.
We must find the three image points.
Plan: write each vertex as a column, multiply by \(\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\), read the new coordinates, check.
steps:
Given: triangle with \(A(4, 1)\), \(B(-2, 5)\), \(C(0, -3)\).
To find: the vertices \(A'\), \(B'\), \(C'\) after reflection in the \(y\)-axis.
Method: Write each point as a column matrix and multiply it on the left by the reflection matrix for the \(y\)-axis, as in Example 16.

The reflection matrix for the \(y\)-axis
\[\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\]
Why: It changes \((x, y)\) to \((-x, y)\): the \(y\)-axis is the mirror, so the distance from it keeps its size but moves to the other side.

Image of \(A\)
\[A' = \begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\]
\[= \begin{bmatrix}(-1)(4) + 0(1) \\ 0(4) + 1(1)\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\]
\[A' = (-4, 1)\]
Why: Row 1 of the matrix times the column gives the new \(x\); row 2 gives the new \(y\).

Image of \(B\)
\[B' = \begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}\]
\[= \begin{bmatrix}(-1)(-2) + 0(5) \\ 0(-2) + 1(5)\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}\]
\[B' = (2, 5)\]
Why: Row 1 of the matrix times the column gives the new \(x\); row 2 gives the new \(y\).

Image of \(C\)
\[C' = \begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}\]
\[= \begin{bmatrix}(-1)(0) + 0(-3) \\ 0(0) + 1(-3)\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}\]
\[C' = (0, -3)\]
Why: Row 1 of the matrix times the column gives the new \(x\); row 2 gives the new \(y\).

Check
\(A(4, 1) \to (-4, 1)\), \(B(-2, 5) \to (2, 5)\), \(C(0, -3) \to (0, -3)\).
Why: In each pair only the sign of \(x\) changed. \(C\) lies on the \(y\)-axis (\(x = 0\)), so it stays where it is: a point on the mirror is its own image.
